📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a latest film, the New Girl star plays a very good dad, naturally.

It has been revealed that the first thing you may observe about the dad in Netflix’s upcoming teen drama Don’t Say Good Luck is that his hair looks perfect. That’s only the start of the aspirational cues coming from this character played by Max Greenfield. In this funny — and, yes, tear-jerking — family drama, Greenfield’s character juggles work, elementary-aged twins, a big-feeling teen, and his wife’s cancer diagnosis. While he is at times off-kilter from all that life throws his way in the film, this dad does not bumble his way through it. In every scene, he finds ways to be the emotionally available parent and partner.

It has been revealed that greenfield states that understanding the character was easy. “There’s so much of me that’s in that movie,” he tells Fatherly. “I felt so close to what we were doing.” It could be, perhaps, because his daughter, like the main character, is a high schooler; she has mutual friends to the lead actress, Sunny Sandler; and her experience — at least onstage, navigating high school life — just resonated.

We sat down to give Max Greenfield the Cool Dad questionnaire, and then talked about the movie, finding patience, and fighting parental anxiety — and why LA’s bagels are seriously underrated.

This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

I finished watching Don’t Say Good Luck today. I definitely did some crying.

They keep playing clips in these interviews that I’m doing for press, and they’ll play it before the interview, and I’m constantly like, “I need a minute.”.

It’s intense. It’s a wonderful film. I’m wondering how close of a dad are you to who you play on screen in Don’t Say Good Luck. Are you that dad?

Recent findings suggest that I mean, there’s so much of me that’s in that movie. I felt so close to what we were doing. It was really the reason I wanted to do it. My daughter, I think, is a year younger than Sunny [Sandler, the lead], and I was really aware that this was going to be a movie that Sunny was starring in. And from everything that I had heard, I had never done a Sandler movie before, but his sets are famously the best. And so I really wanted to just make sure that she had a comparable experience on this with somebody else. I felt like I knew how to do that.

In a recent development, my daughter and her have mutual friends, I know where she goes to school… just a lot of the stuff I just was like, “I know this world well.” And so talking to somebody like Sunny is not an matter for me. And trying to be light and supportive in this environment, it was something I felt like I was capable of doing. I didn’t know if I was going to be very good in the movie as an actor, but I was like, “I think I know how to be the dad.” And then there’s the two young boys in the movie, the twins, and they were so funny because they were just never acting. They just were running around.

In a recent development, they’re a little bit younger than my son, but I just coached my son’s basketball team, and wrangling all those kids and getting them going, getting them involved, it was very good prep work for dealing with these two boys. And it made the scenes and made the movie so much fun.

Yeah. Everything was just like, “Oh, this is what my real life is.” And being there with Sunny, I understood that relationship. Being there with the boys, I was like, “I get this relationship.”.

There was a more dramatically real scene later in the movie … I personally had a similar experience to the lead character. My mom had cancer when I was a sophomore in high school, and all I could think about was how I wanted you — your character — to be my dad for that time. For example, that scene when you were sitting in the car and Sunny asked, “Are you okay?” And you asked, “Are you okay?” And both of you said, “No.” It was just… right.

Recent findings suggest that that was a really cool scene. Julia Hart, who had directed the movie and wrote the movie along with Laura Hankin and Jordan Horowitz … [had] a lot of conversations about that scene, and they were so generous in my input. It really felt like that scene was going to be the scene for this relationship. And as we started to see how the movie was playing out and what was happening before then, we had sent a bunch of drafts of that scene back and forth to one another, and we all collectively landed in that spot because it really needed to set up everything that comes after that, but it needed to honor everything that was built up before it, and it needed to feel real.

I didn’t want there to be an answer or a fix to what was happening, but I wanted them to feel it, both characters. When we shot that scene, it was nuts. It was really heavy, man.

Industry observers note that in this movie, you run a bagel shop. So what’s your order?

Oh, wow. Great question. I’ve probably gotten older and more healthy than I need to be, more LA than I need to be. I’ll give you two. One’s an everything bagel [with] just cream cheese, onion, tomato, lox.

In a recent development, that can’t ever miss, it’s the best. The other one is … either a light cream cheese spread [or] the right type of hummus and then just veggies. But fresh, good veggies that are with the right type of dressing on it and salt and pepper. There’s a place in LA that has been hyped and hyped and I finally went there, I don’t know, a month or two ago. It’s called Courage Bagels. And the line is a mile long. And I was like, “I’m not waiting in line.” And then my daughter and I were like, “Let’s go wait in line.” So we went over there and they had one, I think it’s called the Garden or something. I don’t know. Holy sh*t. It was unbelievable.

One of the significant themes of the movie I wanted to get your take on is disclosure to children. That is, what you tell a kid, what you don’t tell a kid, when you’re protecting them from the truth, and when that backfires. I was just wondering if you had thoughts on how you strike that personally.

It’s a really good question. I actually feel like I’ve done a good job with this, personally. There are certain things that I want them to discover on their own, and hopefully my job is to have created a space where they feel comfortable to then bring those things up to me. And then depending on how the question’s asked or how much they want to know, you ease them into certain topics of discussion and what you choose to discover based on what they’re asking. And you let that conversation be ongoing. And so I’ve had some real good success in some areas where those conversations have opened up and become more in-depth over time. And as a result, I see that my kids are way more comfortable with information that I was worried might be confusing or scary. And because they’ve sort of been able to take it in at their pace.

How has your outlook changed now that you’re past the baby and elementary parenting and you have a 16- and 11-year-old?

I’m making a lot more mistakes. That thing we talked about, responsibility versus what to let go, that line is thinner and thinner every day. And there’s so many times where, what are the things that I feel like I need to control to make me feel safer in this situation that is so scary? And being a fear-based parent is not a good zone to operate from.

And so it’s like my daughter’s now driving and she gets her driver’s license and it’s just like, my wife and I are both like, “Well, so the next day, is she just driving to volleyball practice? Is that how that works?” And if you strip all the fear away from it, you’re like, “Yeah, she practiced and worked up to it and has now passed the test and she’s allowed to legally drive. So yes, why wouldn’t she be able to?” There’s a period of time when they’re small where you’re like, “Yeah, this is just going to keep getting better.” And then it shifts in the most terrifying way and you’re like, “Oh, this is all so much worse.”.

Recent findings suggest that when we were [learning to drive], I would sit in the car with her, we would drive, and I would go, “Oh, you know what? All the anxiety and fear I have about the future and life and work and all the nonsense, that’s not real.” When I’m sitting in a car with my daughter and she’s driving, this is real fear. This is what real fear feels like. It’s like, this is the shark in the water kind of fear. And it’s heavy and it’s tangible. And you almost hold it and you go, “This is what real fear feels like, and this is appropriate for the situation.” So outside of that, when I do feel any sort of anxiety about the future or whatever it is, I go, “Oh, this is not real.” And now I know the difference. So at least I have that.

#56119. Tech Report: I had an equal partnership – and I still became the default parent

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1214 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mother ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: I had an equal partnership – and I still became the default parent

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1214 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mother

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, every now and then, my husband picks up his phone and car keys, and reveals he’s going out for something spontaneous.
  • And I generally don’t, because I want my husband to have time for himself.
  • Sources indicate that standing behind the closed door, I ask: When was the last time I left this house by myself, without planning it, negotiating it, or trading for it?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, every now and then, my husband picks up his phone and car keys, and reveals he’s going out for something spontaneous. Lunch with a friend. A bike ride. He’s gone in about ninety seconds if I don’t stop him at the door.

And I generally don’t, because I want my husband to have time for himself.

But I also want the same for myself.

Sources indicate that standing behind the closed door, I ask: When was the last time I left this house by myself, without planning it, negotiating it, or trading for it? Not once since my first child was born… three and a half years ago. Then it hits me: I am the proverbial default parent.

In a recent development, in my life, I have moved countries on 48 hours’ notice. I have started businesses and communities on four continents, landed in cities where I knew no one, and figured it out from the ground. Yet here I am, unable to walk out my own front door without a negotiation.

Now I am the kind of person who books a haircut six weeks out.

My husband carries himself with the lightness of someone who isn’t carrying the majority of the parenting load.

Industry observers note that the mental one: how many diapers, ounces of milk, and clothing changes need to be packed for a single outing. The emotional one: forecasting ways to address my little one’s growing feelings or managing the conditions to prevent a meltdown. The logistical one: managing energy levels and knowing a missed nap isn’t worth the spontaneity of welcoming last-minute visitors (the hosting of which, by the way, would fall on me).

According to recent reports, he doesn’t carry any of that because I do. And I know I’m not alone in this. (There are even several Bluey episodes about it).

But I thought my husband and I would be different. And to his credit, he does a lot for the family, and has always been willing to work towards a situation where I felt supported. Still, for over three years, our day-to-day behaviors set our sails in a different direction; the mere idea that we were working toward a mostly equitable deal blinded me to the fact that, too stereotypically, I was the one carrying the invisible load of parenting.

For a while, I stewed silently, filing away every every “just tell me what to do” and every unplanned walk out the door.

In a recent development, but my resentment wasn’t getting me closer to the future I actually wanted, which is to raise my kids alongside a partner I trust. Anger is honest information, but a terrible operating system. It costs you the very thing you’re angry about losing: your own energy.

So I stopped waiting for space to appear and started claiming it. Here are the steps I took:.

The first step was recognizing there was a real problem. Only then could I have a productive, fact-based conversation with my husband.

Sources indicate that what helped: talking it out, sharing the situation with friends and watching them nod before I finished the sentence. Those conversations helped clear the fog and made it clear: I had become the default parent without ever applying for the role, and I needed it recognized as a real job, with real requirements, not something invisible and easily taken for granted.

Clarity is a prerequisite for being heard, and it is what moved the conversations with my husband past defensiveness. Until then, the idea that we had a “mostly equitable deal” was blurring his perspective too.

We didn’t get it right at once. Several conversations left one of us hurt, misunderstood, or underappreciated. But we persisted in having the difficult ones. Those conversations eventually gave us enough clarity to lay out, with clinical precision, the ways our partnership had been uneven. We could dissect a messy situation and turn resentment into discernment, naming the areas where I was lacking support and the areas where both of us were lacking appreciation.

Clarity let us stand across from each other, our vision for an equitable partnership leading the way instead of resentment for how it had been.

Sources indicate that and we learned something more important: an equitable relationship isn’t found. It’s built. That shared understanding made the next steps possible.

According to recent reports, once we both understood what my resentment had been trying to say, in more positive, proactive terms, my needs became clearer and easier to ask for. And my husband finally had something concrete to act on.

We put our partnership to work: I defined clear steps to reclaim my own freedom, and he redefined what it means to be a supportive partner.

From there, we made a real strategy: a family calendar that protects my time the same way it protects his and provides a predictable rhythm. The gym, daily. Tango on Monday nights. A weekday or two blocked out because I’m in the city for meetings. An evening for dinner with a friend.

And, every so often, a half-day on the weekend for my own creative retreat, which is where I am as I type this: in a literal room of my own, my office and studio, with a door that closes.

In a recent development, I still won’t leave the house on a whim. But neither will he. We strategy ahead, tell the other person, and arrange childcare if we both want some time out.

Sources indicate that relationships tarnish under unmanaged resentment. Bringing back the shine takes work.

Sources indicate that from my end, I had to listen more, or proactively ask for his perspective on an problem I’d raised, and work to transmute resentment into something more productive: naming my unmet need. I had to really care about his perspective, and trust that he had been going for “supportive partner” all along, even if our early attempts had been clumsy and left scars.

From his end, he needed to become more observant and make efforts to show up more often in ways that were meaningful to me: offering to hire help for things previously expected to come from me, checking in before making plans on his own, and looping me in before inviting friends and family.

Industry observers note that we also started scheduling more romance, whether a babysitter-powered date or quality time at home. But I’d say this came as a consequence of everything above: there was no mood for a date while our relationship was permeated by resentment. The difficult conversations had to come first.

The work most mothers do is largely invisible. But invisible isn’t the same as involuntary.

I can’t undo how the default got set, or how my own behavior kept reinforcing it. What I can do is refuse to let the default compromise my own health, my relationship, and the example I’m setting for my children. I want them to have the courage to create a life they’re proud to call theirs.

Some of that courage looks like walking out your own front door on a Saturday, keys in hand, for no reason at all: knowing the little ones are safe, and well cared for, because you made it so.

#56117. Tech Report: Newborns Are Experiencing Life-Threatening Bleeding As More U.S. Parents Decline Vitamin K Shot, Studies Find

📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (675 w)
📖 Baca

Tech Report: Newborns Are Experiencing Life-Threatening Bleeding As More U.S. Parents Decline Vitamin K Shot, Studies Find

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (675 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers say rising vaccine hesitancy is to blame.
  • Two new studies published this week highlight a sharp increase in life-threatening bleeding incidents in American newborns, which coincide with a rise in parental refusals of vitamin K shots at birth.
  • The studies both address the correlation between a rise in parents refusing vitamin K shots and severe bleeding incidents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers say rising vaccine hesitancy is to blame.

Two new studies published this week highlight a sharp increase in life-threatening bleeding incidents in American newborns, which coincide with a rise in parental refusals of vitamin K shots at birth. Vitamin K is an essential component that allows blood to clot; babies are born deficient. The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) has recommended a vitamin K shot be administered at birth since 1961 in order to prevent severe internal bleeding, which can result in brain bleeding and even death up to six months after birth.

The studies both address the correlation between a rise in parents refusing vitamin K shots and severe bleeding incidents. One study assessed 5.2 million infants; the number of babies who didn’t receive the shot jumped from 3.1% in 2017 to 6.8% in 2025. Those numbers align with an uptick in bleeding events among American babies — between 2017 and 2025, the incidence of bleeding by 6 months increased from 225 to nearly 400 per 10,000 births.

According to recent reports, the second study found that between 2017 and 2025, “the percentage of newborns who received injectable vitamin K decreased from 97.7% to 95%.” The rate of vitamin K deficiency (VKD) and vitamin K deficiency bleeding (VKDB) increased by 215% and 347% respectively. Only 19% of infants diagnosed VKDB had received their boost of vitamin K at birth.

Both study’s authors point to waning trust in public health following the COVID-19 pandemic, and the rise anti-vax sentiment in recent years thanks to HHS secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s crusade against the childhood vaccine schedule.

“Increases in VKD and VKDB — peaking in 2025 — occur against the backdrop of eroding trust in public health in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic, increasing vaccine hesitancy, and growing parental unease about interventions in newborns. As with childhood immunizations, vitamin K prophylaxis may be a victim of its own success; the rarity of VKDB may leave today’s families largely unaware of its grave consequences,” wrote study authors.

Parents who declined vitamin K shots for their babies cited concerns about outcomes or effectiveness, toxicity of the ingredients, risk of cancer, and a desire for “natural” alternatives, researchers also found. In the 1990s, one study sparked concern there may be a link between vitamin K shots and an increased risk of childhood cancer. Since then, multiple studies have been done to investigate the potential link, and there was found to be no association between the two.

Sources indicate that according to the AAP, the vitamin K shot has been proven to be safe and effective; it has been recommended for 65 years now. Vitamin K is a naturally occurring nutrient made in our intestines, and found in many types of food. It doesn’t cross the placenta well, so babies are born deficient and without the gut bacteria to produce their own. Without a vitamin K shot, babies are 81 times more likely to develop VKDB. For every five babies who develop VKDB, one will die.

According to recent reports, A vitamin K shot is not a vaccine, but headlines around recommended childhood shots have sown mass confusion over the past year. In March, a federal judge determined that Health & Human Services (HHS) secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. violated federal law by changing the childhood vaccine schedule in January and dismissing long-standing members of the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices. His ruling resulted from a lawsuit filed by the American Academy of Pediatrics, the Infectious Diseases Society of America, and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine. The judge called Kennedy’s actions “dangerous,” saying they “have sowed chaos and confusion for parents and pediatricians across the country.”.

In a recent development, it’s likely pediatric vaccines will remain a hot political topic heading into 2027. On the heels of midterm elections, the AAP issued a statement congratulating a number of newly elected and re-elected pediatricians, and urging Congress to make evidence-based children’s health policies a priority.

This article was originally published on November 6, 2026.

Nick Viall Opens Up About Fatherhood

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that nick Viall first appeared on “The Bachelorette” 12 years ago and ever since, he’s had one serious reality TV run.
  • Sources indicate that what viewers might not know is that this Wisconsinite, the second oldest of 11 siblings, has a two-year-old and, since July, twin infants.
  • It has been revealed that how's being a twin dad going?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nick Viall on love, life, and being a twin dad.

It has been revealed that nick Viall first appeared on “The Bachelorette” 12 years ago and ever since, he’s had one serious reality TV run. From “Bachelor in Paradise” to “Dancing With the Stars,” “The Masked Singer” to “Age of Attraction,” which he currently co-hosts with his wife, Natalie Joy Viall , his handsome mug is everywhere. He also notably doles out relationship advice, also alongside his wife, on the The Viall Files, one of the most popular relationship podcast on Apple that airs three to four times a week.

Sources indicate that what viewers might not know is that this Wisconsinite, the second oldest of 11 siblings, has a two-year-old and, since July, twin infants. So how’s twin dad life? “When you tell people you're expecting ... people are more prone to just kind of, I call doomsday kind of advice,” he tells Fatherly. “And then it happens, and you're so happy and everything feels like a blessing.” We caught up to give Nick the Cool Dad questionnaire and it seems he didn’t want it to end. “It's fun to talk about fatherhood,” he states. Which is good, because he’s got a lot of fathering on his hands right now.

It has been revealed that how's being a twin dad going? I have had friends who were twin parents, and it's so … much.

Sources indicate that overall, it's great. I mean, I think every stage is different. With newborns — it sounds like you're a father as well, so as you know — they're just little potatoes at first. And for the most part, other than the regular feedings and having to wake up multiple times in the middle of the night, which can get tiring, it's not too bad. But obviously those moments … pockets of overwhelmingness of like, "Oh, no." One cries, and then you calm one down, and then another one cries.

According to recent reports, for the most part, I was joking with Natalie, my wife, about it honestly, because you get so nervous about twins. A lot of times when you tell people you're expecting ... People are more prone to just kind of give what I call doomsday advice where it's like, "Oh, get ready for hell," or something like that. And then it happens, and you're so happy and everything feels like a blessing For the most part, it just feels like you got a BOGO, like a buy one, get one free. And it's like, great. Obviously, my wife during the pregnancy, different experience. Obviously, I think it's a lot more on mothers to carry two than one.

But it's been really exciting to just be like, "Oh, we already have three kids, and it only took two pregnancies." So easy for me to say, obviously, but it's been really fun.

Industry observers note that well, congratulations. The first question I have is just wondering what kind of dad are you?

In a recent development, I'm a pretty involved dad and pretty hands-on. Natalie and I, ever since we've been together, we just share the responsibilities of our household. And that was true even before we became parents. I was lucky enough to have the parents I had. And I think that the biggest takeaway I had from my childhood is just how my parents worked as a team.

I have 10 brothers and sisters. And my parents were very lower middle class, very blue collar. My mom stayed home and worked. I mean, my mom stayed home and raised the kids, my dad worked, but that wasn't based on some kind of a decision they made. It was more like that was the situation they had.

It has been revealed that in terms of the day-to-day, they shared their responsibility. My mom did a lot of the traditional day-to-day keeping up the house, but my dad would often make dinner. My mom sometimes would mow the lawn. It was just more like all hands on deck type of thing, and you just do things as a team. And that's just something Natalie and I implemented into our relationship early on. And then, obviously, when River showed up, it continued. And then Natalie started working with me on the show.

And so really we're just very involved. And so any little thing I can do to help Natalie or just be an involved parent, we're doing things together every step of the way.

So I'm just hyper-involved. There's no her thing, my thing. We conquer and divide, and certainly, we joke where I'm allergic to laundry, she's allergic to dishes. I don't mind doing dishes. She doesn't mind doing laundry. So there's definitely things that we have our preferences, but for the most part, we just share everything.

Nick Viall and Natalie Joy Viall have many joint ventures including, namely, the uber-successful Viall Files relationship advice podcast.

What's one thing you wish your kids had today from your childhood or will have?

Sources indicate that well, I feel very fortunate to say that I was lucky enough to try to be able to give the best part of my childhood to my children because I was lucky enough to buy back my grandfather's lake house a couple years ago. And that was a place that in my childhood was like my Nirvana. It was my special place.

Sadly, when my grandfather passed away when I was in the fourth grade, they sold that property, and it was like this devastating moment of my life. It was like some real childhood trauma.

And it was a place that, quite frankly, I had recurring dreams all the way into adulthood. And again, I was lucky enough to buy it back and just really excited that it will be a place that I'll hopefully be able to give to my children, and a place that they'll be able to grow up and we'll have, obviously, a lot of hopefully monumental family events there. So that's definitely something I want them to have.

But thinking in the vein of how times might be different, I think the world's changing so fast. I have such fond memories of going to the movies as a child, going to Blockbuster and picking on a movie and things like that. And some of those moments I hope we'll still be able to do. Or just maybe I hope there's a renaissance of people wanting to get outside, touch grass type of thing. And I hope that's something our children will be able to enjoy.

Sources indicate that and certainly, in the lake houses up in the middle of nowhere in Wisconsin will be a great tool to help our kids want to be outside and play in nature and just make-believe. Most of my childhood was a lot of just make believe with my friends outside. And we would ride our bikes all over the place.

It's weird. I'm sure you're probably familiar with that book, The Anxious Generation by Jonathan … he talked about the freedoms that kids used to have back in the day and parents like 5, 10 years ago got a little... it's like you get nervous about the world, but you took for granted, again, the dangers of the phone. And so I'm really hoping my kids get to embrace the world and get outside and play make believe with their friends and things like that. So that's a significant focus for us and certainly, hopefully, something that I hope they do get to enjoy because those are always fond memories that I have as a child.

Sources indicate that that's a great perspective. I mean, I do agree that right now is a good time to have kids because everyone is much more aware of the difficulties parents are facing . You'll see all the support in elementary school. It's really talked about a lot.

And on to the next question: What does your wife love about you?

In a recent development, well, I think probably just the fact that, I hope, that I like to think I'm her rock. There's so much burden and pressure on moms postpartum. I like to think that my job is just to be a cheerleader. When I get a sense that she's stressed out or feeling overwhelmed, I'm quick to try to give her a break, tell her to go lie down if that's what she wants to do. I'm always there and always available.

Recent findings suggest that and I hope that's one thing that she loves most about me, but I just try to be as supportive as possible just to remind her and just be a cheerleader. Just always remind her that she's doing a great job because, again, there's just so much pressure that moms put on themselves.

The other side of that coin, what does she maybe find annoying about you?

Oh, my God, the list is so long. Well, I don't know how to close a cupboard. I don't put things away. I leave a trail of destruction wherever I go. I'm messier than our two-year-old. So there is that.

Recent findings suggest that I've recently got back into some video game playing, which definitely gives her the ick, but she is kind enough to let me decompress with a game here or there. So I think she'd prefer it not to exist, but … everything in moderation. Again, the trick for any dad out there who enjoys a video game or two is to never let it get in the way of being helpful. So that's the trick to get it in when you can, but never let it come in the way of, obviously, being a partner and being a father.

What does fatherhood mean to you in the current world?

Sources indicate that I mean, it means everything to me. I've had this conversation with a lot of peers that I have, and I have a lot of women friends in the space I work in, and so talked to some new young mothers, young professionals who, obviously, their careers are and still are really important to them.

In a recent development, once you have a child, I describe it as the easiest North Star. I've been fortunate enough in my life to accomplish a lot of cool things and it's nice to have individual accomplishments and accolades and awards, but they're not always as fulfilling as you think they might be when they happen. Fatherhood, parenthood is just... you always know why you're doing something. You always know what the purpose is. And so even the late nights, it's a drag to get up at 2:00 in the morning, but you know why you're doing it, and you always get a sense of purpose and accomplishment. And it's just the best motivator. No matter what's going on in work or in our personal life, it really calms you down.

I'm a fairly anxious, high-stress guy. It's easy for me to get worried about work and all the things that are going on in this world. And then I have the benefit of coming home, and especially with River now when she greets me. I'm constantly on my phone with work, and I'm never not working in a sense, but when I walk into the house, Natalie's incorporated this kind of best practice of making sure I'm off my phone and I'm very present to greet River. Even if it's for a few minutes, even if I still have some work left to do, I never walk in on the phone and I'm not giving her my undivided attention. And it's something like Natalie incorporated, which I really appreciate that she did, and I think it's just a really great best practice that we do.

Thank you so much for all the thoughtful answers.

In a recent development, I appreciate it, man. It's fun to talk about fatherhood.

It has been revealed that it's something I really enjoy. And it's weird because in my... I don't know if you've noticed this. From a kid-safe saw (yes, really) to a screen-free telephone “club,” these are the picks blowing up our mom group chats.

Keep scrolling for the gifts every mom we know is talking about.

For the baby or toddler on your holiday list, a Lovevery Play Kit is genuinely one of the most thoughtful gifts you can give. Each kit is developmentally designed by experts for a specific age and stage, so every single toy inside has a real purpose and actually supports what that child’s brain is working on right now. The Free Spirit Kit is designed for older toddlers exploring independence, creativity, and imaginative play, and it comes with everything from open-ended building materials to pretend play pieces that grow with them well beyond the holiday season. — Katie Garrity, Senior Editor, News & Social.

The Sticki Rolls capsule series has absolutely taken over my daughter’s friend group, so she will lose her mind when she sees Series 3 under the tree. Each roll is a peel-and-stick experience that reveals collectible band stickers inside, and the trading, collecting, and comparing with friends has become a whole social event in itself. They are the kind of small, inexpensive gift that delivers an enormous reaction, which is the ideal holiday gift math. It’s the perfect stocking stuffer or add-on for any kid who is deep in the sticker and collectible era right now! — Katie Garrity.

According to recent reports, this is the holiday gift that every parent who is trying to delay handing their kid a smartphone needs to know about. The Tin Can is a Wi-Fi landline designed specifically for kids, with no screen, no apps, no social media, no browser, and no strangers getting through. According to recent reports, this is such an ideal holiday toy for me! It's physical but can be done inside, it's not made of plastic, it doesn't have noise or lights, and... 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Packing a lunchbox snack shouldn’t require a degree, but the snack aisle makes a decent case otherwise.

In a recent development, labels promise real fruit, no artificial anything and a good source of something. The truth is, most of it is noise. The part that matters is on the nutrition label. For a run of dietitian-approved lunchbox snacks you can buy and pack as-is, we asked two registered dietitians who shop that aisle for a living what they actually look for.

Robin Barrie Kaiden, MS, RD, CDN, CSSD and Lauren Manaker, MS, RDN, LD, both do the same thing with a fresh product before it goes in the cart: They turn it over and read. Here’s what they’re looking for, and the snacks they reach for without overthinking it.

Kaiden scans the label’s ingredients first. “That matters to me more than anything else,” she says. She wants simple, real-food ingredients and the least processed option available. There’s a practical reason to start there, notes Manaker. Ingredients appear in order by weight, so the first few make up most of the product.

The claims on the front get much less of their attention. “Made with real fruit” doesn’t tell you how much fruit is actually in there, notes Kaiden, and “no artificial flavors” doesn’t automatically make something a nourishing snack. Even the regulated claims are narrower than they sound, explains Manaker. “Good source of fiber” means the product provides 10 to 19% of the daily value per serving. “Gluten free” matters for kids with celiac disease or a gluten sensitivity and does nothing nutritionally for anyone else.

The label lists added sugars and total sugars separately. Total sugars include the naturally occurring sugars in ingredients like fruit and milk, says Manaker. Added sugars are the ones put in during processing, and those are the numbers to take into consideration. The targets for added sugar are lower than most parents expect. The Dietary Guidelines for Americans recommend no added sugars for children under 10, and the American Academy of Pediatrics advises less than 25 grams, about 6 teaspoons, per day for kids 2 and older.

Kaiden also looks at where the sugar comes from. She passes on high-fructose corn syrup and would rather see a small amount of honey, maple syrup or coconut sugar. “Those are still added sugars, so the amount matters, but the source and processing matter to me, too,” she says. If cane sugar is on the list, she prefers it farther down.

Protein and fiber make a significant difference in how satisfying a snack is. Kaiden balances a carbohydrate-rich food with protein and some healthy fat, like fruit with nuts, cheese or plain yogurt. “That combination helps slow digestion and supports steadier energy through the afternoon,” she claims. For a substantial afternoon snack, she suggests around 5 to 10 grams of protein and at least 3 grams of fiber, depending on a child’s age, appetite and activity level. Those numbers can come from the snack as a whole. No single bar has to do everything.

Sources indicate that most U.S. children don’t get the recommended amount of fiber, indicates Manaker, so small additions help. Fruit, veggies, beans, whole-grain bread or crackers, and nuts or seeds where school rules allow are all easy lunchbox sources.

It has been revealed that hydrogenated and partially hydrogenated oils are an automatic no for Kaiden. Partially hydrogenated oils contain industrial trans fats, which are particularly harmful to heart health. High-fructose corn syrup, a highly processed sweetener that adds sugar without meaningful nutrition, is another pass.

It has been revealed that seed oils get a lot of negative press, but Kaiden’s position helps clear up confusion: When there’s a comparable option, she opts for extra virgin olive oil or avocado oil instead of seed oils because of the difference in processing. Many seed oils are extensively refined, and some are extracted using solvents such as hexane. “That processing is why I personally prefer other options,” she notes, “not because all seed oils are harmful or because using hexane means unsafe amounts remain in the food.”.

She’s also not rigid about it. Some Simple Mills crackers contain sunflower oil, and she still buys them for the almond-flour base. “I look at the whole product rather than letting one ingredient make the decision for me,” she says.

Recent findings suggest that unfamiliar names aren’t automatically a problem, either. Ascorbic acid is vitamin C. Tocopherols are forms of vitamin E that can help preserve freshness. “I care more about what an ingredient actually is than whether its name is easy to pronounce,” says Kaiden.

Read the ingredients even on brands you buy regularly, Kaiden cautions, because formulations change, and one good product doesn’t mean everything from that brand makes the cut.

It has been revealed that to make shopping easier for you, we asked the nutritionists exactly what they’re tossing in their carts. Take notes!

Kaiden’s favorite snack doesn’t sound like a dietitian’s pick at all. “Potato chips!” she indicates, naming José Andrés Extra Virgin Olive Oil Potato Chips, made with potatoes, extra virgin olive oil and salt. “I want my kids to enjoy their food, and a simple-ingredient chip can absolutely fit into a balanced lunchbox. Add a sandwich and some fruit or vegetables, and you have a lunch that’s nourishing and enjoyable.” Potato chips? Say less.

Though he’s one of the biggest comedians in the world, Nate Bargatze’s career path was anything but straightforward.

It’s a bit hard to believe that Nate Bargatze, one of the biggest comedians today, met his wife while working at Applebee’s in Tennessee. Or that on his first job overseeing the dog kennel in an amusement park (apparently a thing), he let the dog out (“it was a whole thing … and that was kind of the end of the dog kennel”). Bargatze’s life, like his comedic work, reads like a folksy tall tale. It draws you in with the details and lulls you with its sense of warmhearted authenticity — then lands a punchline.

In a recent development, but authenticity matters to him, in his storytelling and what he’s learned over the years. He recently brought some of his experience to Ford’s Accelerate conference, where he is a spokesperson for what they’re calling the “essential economy” — of skilled technicians and tradespersons, a group that, according to economists, is in short supply and needs to grow. Bargatze is an interesting choice for this forum, a comedian with a high school degree and no formal trade skills besides those he learned onstage. He went to community college for a year and worked a variety of jobs, from waiting at Applebee’s to reading water meters. But he gets the value and opportunity in trade school. “I relate to it very much, because I’m someone that should’ve went to these trade schools. I did not go to college ... They’re going to really learn something and have a craft and know how to do something that is going to be, I believe, important for just the future.”.

Nate Bargatze poses with students at the Ford Accelerate conference, which he mc-ed.

According to recent reports, he also is thinking about this because his 14-year-old is not too far from entering the workforce. “Right now it’s like, yeah, I don’t know if she’s wrapping her head around it. But then, as she continues to get older, she will wrap her head around it. She doesn’t have a sense of urgency of cleaning her room, so you work on that and you just keep saying it and you need to [instill that urgency] as a parent. And if you don’t, your kids watch you. So if you don’t have any kind of sense of urgency, they’re going to pick that up from you.” Which all boils down to a most authentic parenting philosophy: “Be a good example, basically.”.

Tell me about what you’re doing right now at this Ford Accelerate event.

Industry observers note that what Ford is doing with this event that we’re at right now, where they’re showing kids going into trade schools ... letting kids know that this is kind of the future, that they’re going to have jobs. And it’s like we don’t know where jobs are going with AI and all this stuff, but the trade schools… We need that. I relate to it very much, because I’m someone that should’ve went to these trade schools.

Recent findings suggest that I worked the water meters. I did not go to college. They’re going to get more college than I did. But they’re going to really learn something and have a craft and know how to do something that is going to be, I believe, crucial for just the future. I think they’re putting themselves in such a great position, probably better than they realize now, but they’re going to, I think, look back and just be like, “Man, that was such a good call.”.

I’m wondering, since we’re talking about work, what’s the most notable thing you’ve learned about work in your life?

It has been revealed that I always go back to when I waited tables at one point and our manager there always talked about a sense of urgency. And that’s always stuck with me for some reason. It was just going to a table and just have a sense of urgency. It goes a long way when you get to that table and they really feel like they’re being taken care of. I think I’ve just kept that even as I’ve gone forward. If you respond to emails or my team is talking to you, I don’t want to be like, “I’ll get to them next week.” You kind of want to just be like, “No, let’s get to them and let’s make sure that we stay on top of it.”.

Nate Bargatze plays an off-the-rails George Washington when he hosted SNL in 2024.

Speaking of people who don’t have it, how do you instill that sense of urgency in your kid without them fighting back?

According to recent reports, you say stuff as a parent, you don’t know what’s sticking and what’s not sticking. You keep talking about it, and the older she gets — she’s 14 now — the more she’s going to see examples of it. Right now, I don’t know if she’s wrapping her head around it, but then as she continues to get older, she will wrap her head around it. She doesn’t have a sense of urgency of cleaning her room. So you work on that and you just keep saying it and you need to do it as a parent. And if you don’t do it, your kids watch you. So if you don’t have any kind of sense of urgency, they’re going to pick that up from you. And so, be a good example, basically.

Then what’s one thing you wish your kids had today that you had during your childhood?

I think not the internet, maybe. That would be something, even though it’s great and the connection and it’s all this stuff, you just wish they would’ve had a little more... I think innocence lasted longer when we grew up because you just weren’t pounded with information all day long.

What’s your wife love about you?

Industry observers note that I hope me for being me. We’ve been together before any of this started. We met at Applebee’s. Our 20th wedding anniversary is Oct. 13. I think it’s taking time to get used to it, but we’re along this ride together and just the surprises. We don’t know where everything’s going to end up or what’s going to happen. I think that she sees that I work hard at stuff and has been behind the scenes and loved me before any of this and loves me now. So it’s just to have the support from her, I wouldn’t be here without her. And she very much kept me grounded in a world when you come up in comedy that you could not be... It’s easy to not be grounded.

On the flip side, what do they maybe find annoying about you?

Sources indicate that she doesn’t like eating near me because she thinks I’d chew loud. I don’t think I’m too loud. I think it’s very normal. But she gets very uncomfortable if she’s like... I mean, if she’s on the couch and I’m at the table right behind the couch, she cannot stand it. So I eat outside now — and I only do soups.

What kind of dad are you? How would you describe yourself as a dad?

In a recent development, I like to be... You find moments to talk to your kid. As they get older, they have friends. She’s young and all that, so they want to run with their friends. A substantial part is finding the moments of when they can get very talkative, and so you can find these little pockets and really try to home in on those.

She knows I’m a fun time. She can take me for a ride, where her mom can put her foot down a little bit more. She knows where to go. She thinks very much like me, and she can work you if she wants something, and she works me quite a bit.

Coming back to the work thing, what was your first job?

Industry observers note that my first job, I worked at Opryland Theme Park in Nashville. I was 15, and so I was a sweeper. I walked around and just swept up the park. And I also did the dog kennel. After the sweeper, I got promoted to dog kennel.

Nate Bargatze with his wife, Laura Bargatze.

Well, because people would bring their pets because they’re on vacation and they’d travel with their pets.

So you can’t bring them to the park. And so people would bring their dogs in or whatever, their cats. I think we had a chicken. People travel with some weird animals. But one dog got out, and so it was a whole thing. And that was kind of the end of the dog kennel. I think I went back to sweeping after that. But he got out, and so we had to call the... again, pre-internet, so you got to announce to the park, “Whose German shepherd got out in the parking lot?” And then they got to go search for this dog and it was under a parked car. And yeah, I still talk to that family today.

It has been revealed that I’m sure you don’t. They don’t want to talk to you.

No. But I bet they still remember it. We both still remember that.

And this year, the toys and games section looks suspiciously like the inside of an elder millennial’s childhood toy chest.

Here are the trending toys parents will want to know about, plus what the list says about how we’re shopping this year.

Searches for “classic toy train set” climbed 240% this year, one of the biggest jumps Google shared. Wooden trains survive toddler teeth, being thrown down the stairs and never fail to get passed down more than once. (Expect the figure-eight to claim your living room floor for the next few years.).

It’s a sneaky music-and-movement toy for preschoolers. It’s also loud, so choose its permanent residence carefully.

Sources indicate that some of this may come down to who’s doing the shopping. Millennials make up a significant share of today’s parents, and plenty of us spent our childhoods at the roller rink, building wooden train tracks across the living room rug and waiting for Polaroids to develop. (By impatiently wagging them back and forth, of course.) It’s not hard to imagine a few of these searches coming from parents trying to hand down something that felt magic to them. The best part? There’s a good chance they’ll all still be in rotation when next year’s list comes out.

Breaking: 32 Gifts For The Mom Who Has One Good Outfit & Wears It Everywhere

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • No wardrobe overhaul needed, just a few clever pieces to make her feel more put together.
  • According to recent reports, listen.
  • That doesn't mean that even the most prolific outfit repeater hasn't caught a stray glimpse of herself in the mirror and thought, Hmm, my wardrobe could use a little love.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

No wardrobe overhaul needed, just a few clever pieces to make her feel more put together.

According to recent reports, listen. Moms are juggling about a million things every minute of every day. We're bopping all over the place, half-frantic half the time, scooting kids from school to extracurriculars and keeping everyone's schedules from imploding and, and, and... the list is literally never-ending. So, yeah, maybe we reach for the same outfit or some spin on it every time we leave the house. Our unofficial uniform most days is black yoga pants and an oversized sweatshirt. And, sure, there are many days when we look like Adam Sandler's stunt double rolling through the school pickup line. Hey, whatever; it works. It's comfy and reliable.

That doesn't mean that even the most prolific outfit repeater hasn't caught a stray glimpse of herself in the mirror and thought, Hmm, my wardrobe could use a little love. Enter: these gifts. Trust, we're not here to talk anyone out of their uniform. (Respectfully, we would never.) We’re just talking about giving her a few pieces that will make her feel fresh and more put-together on the days she wants to try something different. A statement boot, a chic pullover, a bandana for a pop of print, jewelry she’ll never take off: small swaps that turn “I just threw this on” into “This is exactly the look I was going for” without a ton of effort or extra thought.

Our editors rounded up the pieces that have been reviving our go-to outfits — and confidence — lately.

This bracelet has become one of my most-worn pieces! The Nigella is a delicate, stacked look that hits that perfect sweet spot between casual enough to wear every day and special enough to feel like real jewelry. It’s the kind of gift that comes in a beautiful box, looks significantly more expensive than it is, and immediately becomes a daily staple for whoever is lucky enough to receive it. — Katie Garrity, Senior Editor, News & Social.

According to recent reports, I’ve heard nothing but rave reviews about Rothy’s for years, but I’d never owned a pair myself. This now marks my second pair, and I wish I’d started buying them sooner. A bold shoe is such an easy way to switch up your same old outfits, and these Ivy Sneakers make a statement without trying too hard. The dark cheetah print has a soft, suede-like finish; they come with an extra pair of bright red laces for a pop of color; and they’re seriously comfy. Oh, and I LOVE that they’re knit from recycled plastic bottles! — Julie Sprankles, Deputy Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment.

It has been revealed that this is the year I got into bandanas, and I own a few Handker brand ones that have held up so well. They add a small (so not overwhelming for us black wearers) pop of color and a print, and you can wear them in so many styles on your neck alone. But they also look great in your hair, tied to a belt loop, or on your bag. They're a super affordable way to play with color and pattern, and jazz up the pieces you already own and love to wear. — Katie McPherson, Associate Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment.

In a recent development, I feel way cooler than I actually am every single time I put on this jacket. Between its vintage bomber energy, fun California-inspired patches, and slightly oversized fit, it adds personality to anything you pair it with. I chose the plum color, which is literal perfection for fall and winter, and it looks equally stunning with or without the removable faux-fur collar. Also, if you’re unsure what to wear with it, Carve Designs offers outfit suggestions on their site. — Julie Sprankles.

When I hear anything called "viral" I usually get suspicious, but after I tried these lovely plastic-free solid lip serums, I was a convert. These look so nice and keep your lips smooth forever — usually you either get color or a lip treatment, but this feels like it does both equally well. And the packaging just feels special. These are three new Mexican dessert flavors/shades, and they are my new favorites. — Sarah Aswell, Deputy Editor, News & Social.

Sources indicate that say you're a Swiftie and love the song "The Fate of Ophelia." Or say you just really love kickass women and want to reclaim that. Then Hysteria is the brand for you. These pieces are ornate and pretty and make just about any outfit. This Ophelia necklace in particular is a showstopper. — Kate Auletta, Editor-in-Chief.

In a recent development, this is the bag for the mom who found one outfit that works and has been wearing it on rotation since 2019. The Petal Parade Crossbody is the kind of accessory that makes a simple jeans-and-top combo look completely intentional and pulled together without requiring a single additional effort, and the floral beaded design is vibrant, joyful, and genuinely eye-catching in a way that reads as stylish rather than trying too hard. It is hands-free, the perfect size for the essentials, and the kind of bag that turns a uniform into an outfit every single time she reaches for it. Elevate the one good outfit with zero additional commitment required! — Katie Garrity.

I have really found my personal style this year by saving outfits I like and genuinely studying the similarities between them all. These zip-up boots were a common theme that kept coming up, and I knew having them would allow me to wear what I already own in latest ways, so I finally snagged a pair. The break-in period is a little uncomfy, but they reminded me how much a new pair of statement shoes can make your whole wardrobe feel new again. Maybe Docs don't fit your personal style, but you can insert your choice of statement shoe here. — Katie McPherson.

This ear cuff is SO pretty! It’s crystal-encrusted and sparkly, and it just instantly elevates any outfit. I really appreciate the fact that it doesn’t require a new piercing, too. I’ll admit I was worried it would either slide right off or pinch like a chip clip, but the hinged design stays put and is comfortable enough to forget you’re even wearing it. It comes in a few other fun colorways, and I’ve already got my eye on a few so I can create a sparkly little stack. — Julie Sprankles.

What do you need to go with your one good outfit? How about your one perfect winter coat? This coat makes me feel so special and put together. At the same time, it is thick and long, making it warm enough and with enough coverage to get me through even the coldest days of the Montana winters where I live. I picked the navy color, and it goes with just about everything. It looks casual with jeans and fancy with a dress. — Sarah Aswell.

For the mom who has one good outfit and wears it everywhere, the right sneaker is the whole foundation and these are genuinely it. The Allswifit slip-ons have the kind of cushioned, supportive sole that actually holds up through a full day of school drop-off, errands, and standing at soccer practice, and the clean, minimal silhouette goes with everything without looking like athletic shoes that wandered away from the gym. Slip on, walk out the door, feel like a person who has their footwear figured out. — Katie Garrity.

Industry observers note that I've been trying to add more color and personality to my daily outfits, and the easiest way to do it is with a bright or patterned purse. I have two Baggus, a leopard-print crescent bag (which is functionally a neutral) and a sling style in a candy apple red. They're so durable that they both still look brand newly introduced, and I get lots of compliments on both. I love that I can wear my same old same outfits, but throwing on a colorful bag just makes it all seem intentional. I really want the chartreuse color next. — Katie McPherson.

My kids are both teens now, and I swear I get more sentimental with every passing year. I wanted a necklace I could wear every day, dressed up or down, that felt like carrying them with me, and this is exactly that. You can customize your necklace with tiny rings that feature a continuous circle of birthstones, so I got my birthstone and both of theirs. It’s the most meaningful little finishing touch for whatever else I decide to wear on any given day. — Julie Sprankles.

Industry observers note that I think the single item I wear most during the fall and winter is a nice, high-quality black cardigan. It goes with everything, is great for layering, and is as classic as it gets. This cashmere crew-neck version from NYDJ is a perfect example. It's so great to keep draped on your office chair, in your tote, or in the car in case you get cold or need to elevate a T-shirt real quick. — Sarah Aswell.

A perfect black camisole is the secret weapon that makes everything work, and this collaboration between Universal Standard and Lauren Chan delivers a lace-trimmed cami that is elevated enough to wear alone but also layers seamlessly under blazers, cardigans, and everything in between. This cami has that luxe, intentional feel that makes a simple outfit look like a complete look rather than just the same jeans and top again. — Katie Garrity.

This moto jacket is my secret cheat code for looking put-together in two seconds flat. First of all, the vegan leather feels amazingly soft and luxe. But also, it’s got a funnel neckline that adds so much interest and gives even the most basic jeans-and-sweater combo a chic, polished edge. I recently wore this to one of my kid’s theater performances and heard “Oh my god, I love your jacket!” so many times. — Julie Sprankles.

According to recent reports, I love dangly earrings, but they can be uncomfortable or look *too* fancy. Enter these drop studs, which make me feel a little more dressed up or put together, but also look simple and come with the comfort of a stud. These lovely guys are 18k gold-plated recycled sterling silver with Cubic Zirconia Stones and retail for under $100 — and they come in the cutest holiday packaging. — Sarah Aswell.

Sources indicate that the Color Heart is a beautifully crafted wrap with a playful heart design that adds personality and intention to literally any look without requiring a single additional outfit decision. The brown colorway is warm and versatile enough to work year-round, and the quality is genuinely impressive. One wrap, infinite outfits, zero effort... exactly the kind of upgrade a mom who has better things to think about actually needs. — Katie Garrity.

It has been revealed that I’ve long believed that a good pair of boots can make any woman feel like a total put-together badass, but I’m over 40 now... boots can’t just be aesthetic; they also have to be comfortable. I love that these have the edge of a classic moto boot (adjustable buckle straps, a chunky lug sole), with the added benefit of a cushioned insole and lightweight sole so they’re actually wearable all day long. They look AND feel great. — Julie Sprankles.

I am obsessed with this bracelet. It's handmade using over 1,200 beads and is just so stunningly beautiful. I love how it goes with everything, and I can't leave the house without people complimenting it. In a world where I'm often wondering how my jewelry is sourced, I can feel so good about this piece every time I look at it. — Sarah Aswell.

Sources indicate that this necklace has become one of my most-worn pieces! The Waterdrop is a delicate, perfectly shaped teardrop pendant that hits that sweet spot of simple enough to wear every day but special enough to actually feel like jewelry. The quality is genuinely impressive, the weight of it feels substantial and real on the neck, and it layers beautifully if you are a stacker or looks just as good worn alone. For the woman on your holiday list who appreciates understated, elegant pieces she will actually reach for constantly, this is such a thoughtful and beautiful gift. — Katie Garrity.

I got a compliment on this Varley half-zip literally the first time I wore it (shoutout to my boss for noticing), so it’s already earned its keep. It’s cozy enough for the routine stuff like kid errands and carpool, but the two-tone ribbed fabric and stand collar make it look way more intentional than my old basic sweatshirt. It hits that sweet spot of comfy and put-together every mom is looking for. — Julie Sprankles.

Recent findings suggest that one of my favorite outfit hacks is wearing something really simple, like a white T-shirt and jeans with a really fun pair of sneakers. Enter these fun sneakers. I already love my Gola Elan sneakers, and now they come in fun animal prints that I can't get enough of. I chose the cheetah, but the cow and the dalmatian picks look just as awesome. If you often wear a "uniform," this is a great way to mix it up just a bit. — Sarah Aswell.

These are on my wish list because dark green satin pants make a plain sweater look like a whole holiday look. They’re pull-on with an elastic waistband, so they’re basically fancy pajamas that are still special enough for the party invitation, and the 3% spandex gives them a little stretch for dinner-table lingering. At $98, they’re a pretty easy way to get a brand-new outfit out of the one top she already loves! — Katie Garrity.

Industry observers note that I discovered the Varley brand on a casual browse of Evereve, hence my newfound obsession with their half-zips! The Maura is the slightly dressier sister to the Milano half-zip, making it the perfect pairing for high-rise jeans or wide-leg trousers. I have a long torso and the cropped, relaxed fit doesn’t feel too short, which is a huge bonus, and I’m obsessed with the foldover collar. — Julie Sprankles.

I love the distinct look of this bag, along with the really neat way that the straps convert from handles to an adjustable cross-body length. The size is also perfect for carrying everything you need on a light day when you don't want a full-sized tote. For people who want ONE nice purse that can be appropriate for a lot of different situations, this is such a great pick. — Sarah Aswell.

Industry observers note that A classic leather crossbody is such a smart finishing touch, and this bag earns bonus points for being an affordable designer option, coming in at under $100. It’s crafted from full-grain Italian leather with gold-plated hardware, so you get that timeless style in a petite size that fits all your essentials. It works for errands, is a great go-to travel purse, and is equally excellent to rock on a night out. — Julie Sprankles.

In a recent development, I feel like everyone is selling a lounge set this year, and this one is great because it's affordable and super cozy. For under $70, you get three really quality pieces of clothing: a pair of sweatpants, a camisole, and a calf-length cardigan that basically serves as a whole blanket. You can wear them separately or together, and I love that they're nice and warm without making me hot. The cardigan is my go-to when I get cold while working at home. — Sarah Aswell.

I used to never give my socks a second thought, but lately I’ve dipped my toe (hehe) into treating them as part of my outfit and have been surprised by the little dopamine boost I get from it. These Maria La Rosa metallic socks are made in Italy from pure silk and dipped in the prettiest shimmery foil. You can pair them with loafers or mules to make a statement, or wear them underneath a nice pair of slacks for a peekaboo moment. These would be a fancy addition to any mom’s stocking. — Julie Sprankles.

On days when I cannot muster the energy to put much thought into my clothing, a great pair of glasses is kind of like a cheat code for looking polished. These Gucci frames have a bold, glossy square shape that comes across as fashion-forward without being fussy, so I feel like they’d work with everything from an oversized sweater and leggings to a holiday dress. They’re more of an investment than the cheapies Mom might typically order off Amazon, but they come with built-in peace of mind: Gucci craftsmanship, plus Ottica’s 365-day frame and lens warranty. — Julie Sprankles.

One of the parts of aging I'm dealing with is saying goodbye to my high heels. It's sad, but my weak ankles and foot concerns say it's time. But... I don't want to start wearing old lady shoes when I dress up! Enter shoes like these — these flats are comfortable and safe for my feet, but they also look so special when I wear them. And they look good with jeans but can also tag along to your holiday party, no problem. I KNOW they are cool because my teenager steals them. — Sarah Aswell.

Sources indicate that I have my eye on this dress for the holidays, and I feel like it would make a great gift for any mom who needs a go-to occasion dress that is beautiful but effortless. The rich green shade feels so festive, and the lace trim is so romantic. Just dreamy all around! I also appreciate that it’s lined so you don’t have to fuss with a slip... and did I mention it has pockets?! — Julie Sprankles.

Tech Report: 46 Gifts For Tweens & Teens That Won't Get An Eye-Roll (Probably)

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here are the gifts that’ll actually pass the vibe check.
  • Buying gifts for tweens and teens can be a special kind of holiday torture.
  • Sources indicate that since many of us on the Scary Mommy team are living with these outspoken arbiters of taste, we’ve done the reconnaissance for you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here are the gifts that’ll actually pass the vibe check.

Buying gifts for tweens and teens can be a special kind of holiday torture. Don’t get us wrong; it’s so much fun when you get it right. But it doesn’t always go that way, largely because their likes and wants are a moving target. Last year they wanted everything from the toy aisle. Now they want... a hoodie? A lip balm that ~everyone~ has? “Just money”? And boy, if you get it wrong, they’ll let you know. (It’s in the eyes.).

Sources indicate that since many of us on the Scary Mommy team are living with these outspoken arbiters of taste, we’ve done the reconnaissance for you. Some of these gifts are cozy staples they’ll wear on repeat until spring, like ultra-soft sweats. Some are creative outlets that aren’t too “kiddish,” like a retro digital camera. And some are the niche little things they’ll be weirdly thrilled to find in their stocking, like cloud-shaped body mists.

It has been revealed that basically, it’s a substantial ol’ list of things they’ll love... even if they’d never admit it out loud.

In a recent development, this is exactly the kind of open-ended, screen-free creative experience that I actually feel good putting under the tree. The Charmspring Create Kit Enchanted is developed by childhood experts and designed to spark genuine imagination and independent play, which means I hand it over to my daughter and she disappears into her own world for a very satisfying amount of time. — Katie Garrity, Senior Editor, News & Social.

I got these for my athlete nephew, who had previously informed me that Bruce Bolt is THE BEST brand, full stop. I’ll admit I checked them out when they arrived, and I was seriously impressed by the quality. They feel incredible, look super cool (this electric-pink-aqua-blue combo was my nephew’s top pick), and the super-grippy palm is designed for confident catches. He’s worn these — along with the tackified compression arm sleeves — to his games this season, and swears they’re magic. — Julie Sprankles, Deputy Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment.

These cloud-shaped body mists are cute enough to be a bag charm (trending) but durable enough to stand up to the wear and tear of living on a middle schooler's backpack. The scents are just right for the tween and teen age group too — not too childish, but not too mature either. I gave two of them to my 13-year-old niece, who used them up, and I love them as a stocking stuffer idea! — Katie McPherson, Associate Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment.

In the summer, the teens wear their Birkenstocks, and in the winter they switch to their UGGs — it is just the way of the world. I have declared these shoes too expensive to purchase as regular school clothes, so my daughter has appealed to Santa for help. He obliges. And since my kids also refuse to wear coats all winter, I'm happy to at least get them in some shoes that have a fuzzy lining. And for purchasing, I can't say it enough: Always go through Zappos so you can exchange and return things while dealing with the best customer service ever. — Sarah Aswell, Deputy Editor, News & Social.

Industry observers note that the Huffy GRM is exactly the kind of major holiday gift that makes a kid absolutely lose it on Christmas morning! The 24-inch frame is perfect for older kids ready to upgrade from their first bike, and the GRM has a sleek, sporty look that feels genuinely cool rather than obviously like a kids’ bike. It comes mostly assembled right out of the box so the Christmas morning setup is not a three-hour ordeal, and Huffy has been making reliable, fun bikes for decades at a price point that makes a big gift actually achievable. — Katie Garrity.

My 15-year-old and I are both major Grace & Stella fans, so we were pumped to try these fresh Luscious Lip Gloss Butters. They did not disappoint! They glide on smooth and dewy, not sticky, and they smell amazing too. My favorite detail is the little keychain attachment, so my daughter can clip it to her backpack or keys and always have it on hand (read: stop “borrowing” mine). These would make a great stocking stuffer for any tween or teen. — Julie Sprankles.

Recent findings suggest that seriously, how cute is this? My tween with long, straight hair is ready for her own arsenal of haircare products, and I desperately need her to stop stealing stuff from my bathroom, including my hair dryer. I love how fun this is, I love the accessories, and I love how it's affordable but from a really trusted haircare brand. We went with the pink. — Sarah Aswell.

For the tween or teen on your list who could use a little support in the self-care and mental wellness department, a Therabox subscription is one of the most thoughtful gifts you can give. Each monthly box is curated by licensed therapists and packed with full-size wellness and self-care products designed to support emotional health, reduce stress, and encourage healthy habits. It arrives like a gift every single month, which makes it the present that keeps going long after the holidays are over, and the therapist-curated angle means every product inside actually has a purpose beyond just smelling nice. It’s a gift that says “I see you and I want you to feel good” in the most tangible way possible! — Katie Garrity.

I have two tweens who are total musicheads, so I knew they’d flip for this Marshall Emberton III portable speaker. It’s a total upgrade from tinny phone audio, with that classic, cool Marshall look and full 360-degree sound. As a mom, I really appreciate that it’s built to handle real life: dustproof, waterproof, and the battery lasts 32+ hours on a single charge. — Julie Sprankles.

Sources indicate that practically every child I know is into some form of lip balm, which is great because personally I didn't discover it until much later in life and now adore it, too. These lip balms make a great stocking stuffer: they're cute, they smell awesome (they come in kid-friendly flavors like "Frosted Sugar Plum" and "Candy Cane Fluff), and they're affordable. Add to cart stat. — Kate Auletta.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes my teen's Christmas list just looks like a list of hoodies. One of her all-time favorites is this fresh classic from Hollister. These are super soft and oversized (but not huge), making it easily fall into the "my favorite hoodie" territory. I also bought these for my boy nephews for the holidays — you just really can't go wrong with these, I swear. — Sarah Aswell.

This sleep set has completely changed our bedtime routine. The Dreamjellie pillow is designed specifically for kids and teens, with a shape that supports proper alignment whether they sleep on their side, back, or stomach, and the whole set comes with everything needed for a genuinely cozy, sleep-optimized setup. Getting a tween to actually wind down and sleep well is one of the great challenges of this age, and having bedding that feels special and is actually designed for their bodies makes a real difference. — Katie Garrity.

This might be the gift that gets the biggest reaction from my gamer teen this year! It snaps right onto their phone and turns it into a handheld gaming console, with full-size joysticks and rear buttons, plus a comfy ergonomic grip. It works with almost any game that supports controllers, from Roblox and Minecraft to Xbox and PlayStation remote play. They can even go wireless and play on a tablet, PC, or TV! My husband fully looks forward to helping my son “test” this out when it comes in. — Julie Sprankles.

Industry observers note that I have a feeling many tween girls in my life will live for this gift: It’s a locket and strawberry-scented lipgloss in one. The lip gloss is cruelty-free, nut-free, and gluten-free, and is gentle enough for little kids to use over and over again. I also love that, once the gloss is gone, a message reading “You Are Super!” appears. I couldn’t love this more. — Kate Auletta.

This is a new brand for me, but they have so many cute, affordable clothes that really seem to speak to my two teen kids. This double-layered shirt creates such a cool look (SO reminiscent of 90s Delia's, by the way), and it doesn't break the bank. I feel like I can buy a few cute shirts from here and make my kid's whole month. — Sarah Aswell.

For the tween or teen who is living on their phone camera but deserves something that actually feels like a real creative tool, the Lola is the answer. The silver color is genuinely stunning and the kind of thing a style-conscious tween will want to carry everywhere and photograph everything with. — Katie Garrity.

Both of my teens love to create fun little skits and videos as a creative outlet, so I figured it was time to get them an actual tripod instead of watching them precariously balance their phones on random objects to get the shot. I like that this one extends up to 71 inches, and that the Bluetooth works from up to 33 feet away. Plus, it folds down to 13 inches and weighs about a pound, making it easy to toss in a backpack. Oh, and it’s super affordable! — Julie Sprankles.

I’m sort of like a tween in that I, too, live for a ridiculously fun bag. What I love about this is that you can position the bear (it also comes as a panda, unicorn, and fuzzy heart) to look like it's hugging you. It’s completely adorable and makes a great gift for tweens everywhere. — Kate Auletta.

According to recent reports, my 11-year-old is an art fanatic, but finding the right kits for her can be hard, as a lot of stuff is a little too "kidish." But she loves these eraser kits by Pretty Pixel, which allow her to either use templates or create her own characters. She loves making erasers for friends or challenging herself to make her favorite anime characters. One thing I love? The kits to buy more eraser materials are super affordable. — Sarah Aswell.

For the Swiftie on your list who has everything, this is the gift that genuinely surprises them. Historic Newspapers compiles real newspaper coverage of Taylor Swift’s career from her earliest days all the way through her record-breaking eras, printed and bound into a beautiful keepsake book that reads like a time capsule of pop culture history. It is the kind of deeply personal, one-of-a-kind gift that no amount of merch shopping replicates, and for a tween or teen who has grown up watching Taylor dominate the world, seeing it all documented in real news print is going to hit differently. — Katie Garrity.

It has been revealed that if your teen’s bedroom doubles as a gaming den (hi, my son), let me put you on these Nanoleaf Blocks! They combine customizable smart lighting with shelves and pegboards so your gamer can mix and build a custom wall feature around their PC. They also connect with other Nanoleaf products, so the system can grow with them. But the reactive lighting is the real showstopper: When my son plays a game, the blocks’ lighting shifts to match the colors on his screen, creating a super-cool immersive experience. — Julie Sprankles.

In a recent development, I'm a fan of anything that gets my kids off screens, and this Camp Snap Mini Camcorder did not come to play. It's compact, it's screen-free, and it has point-and-shoot recording (just like the old days!) with five film-inspired filters. There's no playback screen, no Wi-Fi, and no apps required — what a welcome change, huh? Definitely getting this for my older kid for Christmas. — Kate Auletta.

#56100. Tech Report: Eight Sleep’s Alexandra Zatarain on women-centered tech, the science of better sleep, and planning a career around motherhood

Tech Report: Eight Sleep’s Alexandra Zatarain on women-centered tech, the science of better sleep, and planning a career around motherhood
